title: A repository's .git/config written by something other than git
summary: node (pid 1903747) wrote to /tmp/moat-is-lab-1788556716735-1903747/.git/config. Parent chain: bash -> node.

explain.what: node wrote to /tmp/moat-is-lab-1788556716735-1903747/.git/config, which runs automatically on your next login.
explain.why: .git/config decides where `git push` sends your code and what git runs on your behalf: a rewritten remote URL ships the whole repository to somebody else the next time you push, and a `core.fsmonitor` or `core.pager` entry there is a command that runs on your next git command. The file is small, boring, and nobody reads it during review.

title: Project-local credential file read (.env, .npmrc, .git-credentials)
summary: node (pid 1903747) read /tmp/moat-is-lab-1788556716735-1903747/.git/config. Parent chain: bash -> node.

explain.why: Every other credential rule watches an absolute path under your home directory, and real tokens do not live there: they live in the repository you are working in. A .env beside the code, a project .npmrc with a registry token, a .git/config with the token embedded in the remote URL. A postinstall script reads those with the same permissions you have, and nothing in the rest of this ruleset would see it.

explain.expected: Constantly, and that is the point of scoring it by who is asking. Your dev server, test runner and framework read .env every time they start; that is an ordinary session and stays in the timeline. The same read from inside a package install is what this exists for. Package managers, git, direnv, editors, container tools and backup programs are excluded outright.
next: If you did not expect this: find the process with `ps -fp <pid>` and stop it before it finishes.
Run `npm token list` then `npm token revoke <id>`, and delete the `_authToken` line from ~/.npmrc. If the token could publish, check your packages' recent versions.
Revoke the token at https://pypi.org/manage/account/token/, issue a replacement, and update ~/.pypirc and any CI secret that held it.
Treat every line of ~/.git-credentials as public: each one is a forge password or token in cleartext. Rotate them at their forges and switch to a credential helper that does not store plaintext.
Revoke the token at https://github.com/settings/tokens (or `gh auth logout && gh auth login`), issue a new one, and grep ~/.git-credentials, ~/.netrc and your shell rc files for copies.
Inspect the dropped file before deleting it: `file <path>`, `strings -n 8 <path> | head`, and look its sha256 up before you lose the evidence.

steps.title: A repository's .git/config written by something other than git

chain.summary: 2 things happened in 1 second under node (pid 1903747), crossing persist and cred.

triage.summary: A person at a terminal installed a local lab tarball and imported it three seconds later; the package wrote a 76-byte synthetic .git/config into a throwaway /tmp directory it had just created, pointing at example.invalid. No real repository, credential file or remote was touched.
triage.reasoning: Mechanism end to end. (1) Ancestry: the writing process is node pid 1876167, args `-e import('moat-is-hijack-simulator')`, parent bash pid 581833. process.json shows that node's fds 0/1/2/20/23 are /dev/pts/8 and the parent bash is an interactive shell on the same pts in a herdr pane (HERDR_PANE_ID=w5:p3, SHLVL 1) — a human was at a keyboard, despite moat scoring context as 'unknown'. (2) The same shell pid 581833 ran, 3.1 seconds earlier at 20:41:08.097Z, `npm install --force http://192.168.44.122:8080/moat-is-hijack-simulator-1.0.1.tgz` (alerts.jsonl line 6214, moat-pkg-subtree-interpreter-spawn) from cwd /home/dan/maotjack. Two hand-typed commands in one shell, not an unattended drop. (3) I read the staged copy target.config.suspect, not the live path: it is exactly `[remote "origin"]\n  url = https://MOAT_CANARY@example.invalid/demo/repo.git` — a reserved, non-resolvable TLD, in /tmp/moat-is-lab-1788554471214-1876167/.git/, a directory the same process had just created. No repository of the user's has its remote rewritten; there is no repository there at all. (4) The installed source /home/dan/maotjack/node_modules/moat-is-hijack-simulator/index.js accounts for every observed event: it mkdirs the /tmp lab root, writes a synthetic .npmrc with the literal string MOAT_IS_CANARY_TOKEN and that exact .git/config, reads those two files back (which is the paired timeline alert 01M1Q2ESXJACMACPP40PTSH25T, whose path is the /tmp lab copy — not ~/.npmrc, not a real project), builds a fixed `new Function('return "MOAT_SIMULATION_ONLY"')`, opens a WebSocket, and on exactly one hardcoded message (action=='write_marker' && value=='MOAT_SIMULATION_ONLY') prepends a comment line to its own index.js. Nothing from the socket is evaluated or written anywhere else. (5) net.txt and fd 22 show one socket, ESTABLISHED to 192.168.44.122:4873 — RFC1918, the same host the tarball came from; there is no internet egress. Real data that left the machine is hostname/platform/arch/cpu count/cwd, plus the two synthetic canary strings. (6) /var/log/pacman.log has no transaction anywhere near 20:41 (last activity that evening is the user's own omarchy-moat package builds hours earlier), consistent with this being npm-only and touching nothing system-level. (7) Independent of anything the package says about itself: the user's own moatd source, /home/dan/Projects/omarchy-moat/moatd/src/chain.rs, opens with a design note naming `node -e "import('moat-is-hijack-simulator')"` as the motivating case for the sequence-correlation module being written, with a test `the_npm_hijack_simulation_becomes_one_chain`. This is the author's own detection lab, exercised against his own sensor. I did not rest any of this on the package name, its README, the word 'simulator', or the 'simulation: true' field it sends — those are the package's own claims. What carries the verdict is the tty-rooted ancestry, the actual 76 bytes written into a fresh /tmp dir at a path no git command consults, the single RFC1918 socket, and the absence of any real-credential or real-repo alert from this pid. Residual risk the user should be aware of rather than a reason to withhold: the tarball is unsigned, fetched over plain HTTP from a LAN host and installed with --force, so no package provenance backs it, and it does fingerprint the host to that LAN listener. Deliberately not proposing an allowlist rule: the exe+file scope moat suggests contains a per-run runId path that will never recur, and the exe scope would let any node process write any .git/config — that would blind exactly the detection chain.rs is being written to catch. Ack these, do not ignore them.
recommend: moatctl ack 01M1Q2ESXJACMACPP40PTSH25T   # same lab run: read-back of the synthetic /tmp lab .npmrc/.git config
moatctl ack 01M1Q2EPR1DJD9RMG2PSJW82X3   # the npm install --force of the lab tarball that preceded it
moatctl show 01M1Q2ESWNFRTFES6AR42EG75S --json   # keep as the reference sample for the chain.rs correlation work; do not run `moatctl ignore` on this one
